text: Build a CI queue observability and scheduling layer that records queue wait time per job, per team, and per runner pool, then applies priority rules and autoscaling hints so the longest-waiting onboarding and release-blocking jobs run first.
The CI system exposes queue timestamps and runner-pool metadata through an API or logs; this has not been verified.

Create a flaky-test detection and quarantine service that reruns failures, scores tests by pass/fail variance across identical commits, and flags suspected flakes in pull request and release dashboards without hiding real failures.
Test results are available in a structured format (e.g., JUnit XML) with stable test identifiers across runs.
Offer a release-signal dashboard that separates "failed due to likely flake" from "failed due to deterministic regression," so release managers can judge readiness with explicit confidence levels.
Teams will trust a flake classification enough to use it in release decisions; this likely requires a trial period and calibration against known outcomes.

Provide a golden-path service template catalog with versioned templates, a scaffolding CLI, and automated upgrade pull requests, so teams stop duplicating templates and shared updates propagate in a controlled way.
Existing duplicated templates can be mapped to a small number of canonical variants without breaking team-specific needs.
Add a dependency-update canary pipeline that tests proposed updates against a sample of template-derived services before rolling out to shared templates, with staged rollout and automatic rollback.
A representative sample of downstream services exists and can be built in CI at acceptable cost.
Implement preview environment lifecycle management with TTLs, idle detection (no traffic or commits), automatic suspension, and per-team cost attribution reports.
Idle cost is material relative to other platform spending; no cost data was supplied.

Build a build-cache and container-image analyzer that reports cache hit rates, layer sizes, and Dockerfile ordering problems, then suggests fixes such as base-image consolidation, multi-stage builds, and remote cache configuration.
Build tooling emits enough cache and layer telemetry to diagnose misses; this is unverified.

Prioritize the roadmap in this order: CI queue visibility, then flaky-test handling, then template and dependency tooling, then preview cost controls and build/image optimization, because the operator context says CI queues and flaky tests are the most requested work.
Request volume reflects actual impact; it may instead reflect which complaints are most visible.

Build a "release-signal court" that treats each CI test result as testimony with a learned reliability score, so a release gate asks "how much do we trust this signal?" and not "did it pass?". Flaky tests are down-weighted rather than quarantined or deleted, and the gate reports a confidence interval for release readiness.
Test history is available at a granularity (per test, per commit, per runner) sufficient to estimate reliability; this has not been verified.
Teams will accept a probabilistic gate; many may prefer a binary pass/fail for auditability and compliance reasons.
Flakiness is mostly independent of the code under test. If it correlates with real latent defects (races, timing bugs), down-weighting could hide genuine problems.

Use the reliability model to schedule CI work, running the highest-information tests first and deferring low-information, high-flake tests. This could reduce queue pressure without adding capacity, tying together the two most-requested themes.
Reordering tests does not break implicit inter-test dependencies or shared-state assumptions.
Queue delays come from scheduling and test volume rather than from raw runner capacity; if they are capacity-bound, reordering will help little.

Treat service templates as a package-managed dependency graph, using automated "template drift" pull requests plus a canary rollout of dependency updates across a sample of template consumers before the update reaches the shared template.
Duplicated templates are caused by missing discoverability or customization hooks, not by real divergent needs; forced consolidation could slow teams that legitimately differ.
A representative canary subset of consumers can be identified automatically.

Give preview environments a "lease with decay" model: each environment holds a cost budget that depletes with idle time and is renewed by actual traffic or commits, with a snapshot-and-restore on demand instead of hard deletion.
Snapshot restore is fast enough that developers don't perceive it as a regression compared with always-on environments.
Idle cost is significant relative to other spend; no cost figures were supplied.

Challenge the premise of faster builds by investigating whether cache misses and image size are symptoms of unstable build inputs (non-hermetic steps, timestamps, unpinned layers). A "cache-miss explainer" could attribute each miss to a specific input change and rank root causes.
Build tooling exposes enough metadata to diff inputs between runs.

Build a "release-signal ledger" that treats flaky tests as probabilistic evidence rather than defects to eliminate. Each test result carries a learned reliability weight, and release gates consume a confidence score instead of a binary pass/fail. This is unconventional because it stops chasing flake elimination and makes the platform robust to flakiness.
Flake probability can be estimated per test from historical reruns with enough data, and that data is retained and accessible. This is unverified.
Release owners will trust a probabilistic gate; many organizations may require deterministic gates for audit or compliance reasons.
Flakiness is mostly independent noise. Correlated infrastructure causes, such as a bad runner or a shared dependency outage, would break the weighting model.

Replace queue-scaling work with a "speculative CI" scheduler that predicts which jobs are likely to be irrelevant to a change, using the change's dependency graph, and runs them at lower priority or post-merge. The goal is shorter queues for onboarding developers without adding capacity.
An accurate dependency graph is available for the repository layout. Polyglot or dynamically linked builds may defeat it.
Deferring jobs does not let regressions reach shared branches unacceptably often. The cost of late detection is unmeasured.

Treat service templates as a dependency-managed product. Generate services from a versioned template with an automated "template drift" report and staged rollout of template updates, with canary adoption by a few teams before wide release. This addresses duplicated templates and dependency updates that break shared templates in one mechanism.
Teams will accept staged template upgrades rather than forking, and the duplication is not caused by legitimate divergent needs.
Dependency breakage in shared templates is detectable by pre-release synthetic builds of representative services.
Make preview environments lease-based, with cost-aware expiry that extends only on observed activity such as traffic, commits, or reviewer comments, and posts the running cost to the pull request.
Activity signals reliably indicate that an environment is still needed. Some long-lived demos or stakeholder reviews would be wrongly reclaimed.
Use build-cache and container-image telemetry to attribute cache misses and image bloat to specific commits or Dockerfile layers, then surface a "cache regression" check on pull requests.
Cache keys and layer metadata can be captured without invasive build changes.
